plan.topic_summary: Co-packaged optics (CPO) integrates optical transceivers directly onto or adjacent to the same package as compute or switch silicon, addressing the power and bandwidth limits of electrical interconnects in data centers and HPC. Its commercialization timeline over the next 1–5 years will reshape the semiconductor supply chain across foundries, advanced packaging, and optical component suppliers.

sources.title: Co-packaged optics (CPO): status, challenges, and solutions
sources.abstract: Due to the rise of 5G, IoT, AI, and high-performance computing applications, datacenter traffic has grown at a compound annual growth rate of nearly 30%. Furthermore, nearly three-fourths of the datacenter traffic resides within datacenters. The conventional pluggable optics increases at a much slower rate than that of datacenter traffic. The gap between application requirements and the capability of conventional pluggable optics keeps increasing, a trend that is unsustainable. Co-packaged optics (CPO) is a disruptive approach to increasing the interconnecting bandwidth density and energy efficiency by dramatically shortening the electrical link length through advanced packaging and co-optimization of electronics and photonics. CPO is widely regarded as a promising solution for future datacenter interconnections, and silicon platform is the most promising platform for large-scale integration. Leading international companies (e.g., Intel, Broadcom and IBM) have heavily investigated in CPO technology, an inter-disciplinary research field that involves photonic devices, integrated circuits design, packaging, photonic device modeling, electronic-photonic co-simulation, applications, and standardization. This review aims to provide the readers a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art progress of CPO in silicon platform, identify the key challenges, and point out the potential solutions, hoping to encourage collaboration between different research fields to accelerate the development of CPO technology.

sources.title: 3D optoelectronics and co-packaged optics: when solving the wrong problems stalls deployment
sources.abstract: The rapid growth of AI and accelerator-driven workloads is forcing a fundamental rethinking of optical interconnect architectures in datacenters. Co-packaged optics and three-dimensional photonic integration have emerged as promising solutions to overcome the energy and bandwidth limitations of electrical I/O. Yet, as optics move closer to compute, packaging, thermal management, and system-level robustness increasingly dominate performance and scalability. Here, we argue that co-packaged optics should not be viewed as a component-level optimization, but as an architectural commitment that reshapes the boundaries between photonics, electronics, and system design. We examine how heterogeneous integration strategies, chiplet-based optics, and emerging packaging platforms redefine scaling laws for AI systems, often introducing trade-offs that are underappreciated in device-centric analyses. Looking forward, we discuss why standardization, serviceability, and thermal-aware co-design will be decisive in determining whether co-packaged optics can transition from early deployment to widespread adoption in AI-scale datacenters.

sources.title: Progress in Research on Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: In the 5G era, the demand for high-bandwidth computing, transmission, and storage has led to the development of optoelectronic interconnect technology. This technology has evolved from traditional board-edge optical modules to smaller and more integrated solutions. Co-packaged optics (CPO) has evolved as a solution to meet the growing demand for data. Compared to typical optoelectronic connectivity technology, CPO presents distinct benefits in terms of bandwidth, size, weight, and power consumption. This study presents an overview of CPO, highlighting its fundamental principles, advantages, and distinctive features. Additionally, it examines the current research progress of two distinct approaches utilizing Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Laser (VCSEL) and silicon photonics integration technology. Additionally, it provides a concise overview of the many application situations of CPO. Expanding on this, the analysis focuses on the CPO using 2D, 2.5D, and 3D packaging techniques. Lastly, taking into account the present technological environment, the scientific obstacles encountered by CPO are analyzed, and its future progress is predicted.

sources.title: Next-generation Co-Packaged Optics for Future Disaggregated AI Systems
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics is poised to solve the interconnect bandwidth bottleneck for GPUs and AI accelerators in near future. This technology can immediately boost today's AI/ML compute power to train larger neural networks that can perform more complex tasks. More importantly, co-packaged optics unlocks new system-level opportunities to rethink our conventional supercomputing and datacenter architectures. Disaggregation of memory and compute units is one of such new paradigms that can greatly speed up AI/ML workloads by providing low-latency and high-throughput performance, while maintaining flexibility to support conventional cloud computing applications as well. This paper gives a brief overview of state-of-the-art of co-packaged optical I/O and requirements of its next generations. We also discuss ideas to exploit co-packaged optics in disaggregated AI systems and possible future directions.

sources.title: Co-packaged Optics
Low-Loss Integration of High-Density Polymer Waveguides with Silicon Photonics for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: Co-Packaged Optics applications require scalable and high-yield optical interfacing solutions to silicon photonic chiplets, offering low-loss, broadband, and polarization-independent optical coupling while maintaining compatibility with widely used approaches for electrical redistribution. We present two heterogeneous integration techniques that enable high-density electrical and optical I/O connections, utilizing adiabatic coupling between on-chip silicon nitride (SiN) waveguides and package-level polymer optical waveguides. In the first approach, polymer waveguides are patterned using standard lithography directly on the surface of the photonic chip, ensuring compatibility with chip embedding as commonly employed in chip-first fanout wafer-level packaging. In the second approach, photonic chips are flip-chip bonded to the package substrate. Both techniques have been experimentally validated, achieving a coupling efficiency near 1 dB between SiN and polymer waveguides in O-band, for both TE and TM polarizations. SiN tapers were designed using the "Mono" method to optimize phase-matching conditions between the two waveguides, a critical requirement for integrating diverse optical components. These results demonstrate the potential of polymer waveguides in Co-Packaged Optics applications, achieving sub-2 dB chip-to-chip and chip-to-fiber coupling losses.

sources.title: Glass Substrate for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics leads to significant power reduction by placing the electronic and photonic chiplets in a single package. An integrated electro-optical substrate made of glass with optical waveguides, through vias and electrical redistribution layers inside a single-sided cavity enables fine-line electrical routing and low-cost assembly. Existing glass and thin film technologies were evaluated and combined into a single process stream including photonic assembly. Photonic chips with silicon nitride waveguides were optically coupled to integrated low-loss (<0.1 dB/cm) glass waveguides with minimum loss of 0.65 dB achieved by fiducial alignment and pick-and-place assembly.

sources.title: Machine Learning-Driven Design of Mixed-Pitch Grating Couplers for Co-Packaged Optics Applications
sources.abstract: A mixed-pitch grating coupler which can couple a wide range of wavelengths is preferred in its application in co-packaged optics (CPO). However, the design and optimization of such grating coupler is complex. In this work, we developed software with integrated deep neural network (DNN) model to automatically design the mixed-pitch grating coupler from user-specified peak wavelengths and full-width half-maximum (FWHM) values. We first trained the DNN model with 10,000 rows of grating parameters-power spectrum datasets, where the power spectrum was simulated using finite-difference time domain (FDTD) technique. Upon training, we tested the model using ~1,000 different combinations of peak wavelengths and FWHM values. Among the combinations, 822 attempts have <15% error, while 351 attempts have <5% error when comparing the user-specified and FDTD-verified spectrum. Meanwhile, comparing the user-specified and FDTD-verified peak wavelengths, 844 attempts have peak wavelengths with absolute error (AE) < 2 nm. For FWHMs, 738 attempts have FWHM values with AE < 10 nm. We have also developed a graphical-user interface (GUI) to ease the usage of this software.

sources.title: Glass Platform for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
sources.abstract: Placing the electrical and photonic chiplets in a single package leads to significant power reduction. Chiplets are connected by fine-line electrical routing over a length of a few millimeters and optical interconnects in the package connect photonic chips with optical fibers for off-package communication. A packaging substrate made of glass with optical waveguides, through glass vias and electrical redistribution layers inside a single-sided cavity enables lower-cost assembly. A single-sided 50 μm deep cavity was etched in glass, and electrical copper lines with 5 μm in height and width were deposited on the floor of the cavity. Ion-exchange (IOX) waveguides with propagation loss of <0.1 dB/cm were fabricated below the glass surface. For flip-chip assembly of photonic chips and optical coupling with the IOX waveguides at the top surface of the glass, all electrical interconnects were located inside the cavity. Photonic chips with silicon nitride waveguides were optically coupled to glass waveguides with a minimum loss of 0.5 dB, achieved by fiducial-aligned flip-chip photonic assembly. A low-profile fiber connector with height of 4.4 mm connects the integrated ion-exchanged waveguides with the optical fibers. Average connector loss of 0.83 dB was demonstrated with physical contact between fibers and IOX glass waveguides.

sources.title: C2PO: Coherent Co-packaged Optics using offset-QAM-16 for Beyond PAM-4 Optical I/O
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics (CPO) has emerged as a promising solution for achieving the ultra-high bandwidths, shoreline densities, and energy efficiencies required by future GPUs and network switches for AI. Microring modulators (MRMs) are well suited for transmitters due to their compact size, high energy efficiency, and natural compatibility with dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM). However, extending beyond the recently demonstrated 200 Gb/s will require more advanced modulation formats, such as higher-order coherent modulation (e.g., QAM-16). In this work, we show how microring resonators (MRMs) can be efficiently used to implement phase-constant amplitude modulators and form the building blocks of a transmitter for offset QAM-16, which has been shown to simplify carrier-phase recovery relative to conventional QAM. We simulate and evaluate the performance of our proposed MRM-based coherent CPO (C2PO) transmitters using a foundry-provided commercial silicon photonics process, demonstrating an input-normalized electric field amplitude contrast of 0.64 per dimension. Through full link-level bit error rate modeling, we show that our design achieves 400 Gb/s using offset QAM-16 at a total optical laser power of 9.65 dBm-comparable to that required by conventional QAM-16 MZI-based links, despite using 10-100x less area. We further conduct a thermal simulation to assess the transmitter's thermal stability at the MRM input optical power required to meet a target BER at the desired data rates. Finally, as a proof of concept, we demonstrate 25 Gb/s MRM-based offset QAM-4 modulation with a chip fabricated in the GlobalFoundries 45 nm monolithic silicon photonics process.

sources.title: Heterogeneous Integration in Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems
sources.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) and Large Language Model (LLM) require data center to have higher bandwidth, and better energy efficiency. To achieve this, Co-packaged optics (CPO) is one of the future directions that leverages advanced packaging with integrated photonics. However, this tight integration complicates data center system design and multi-physics interactions, including electrical, optical, thermal, mechanical, and material aspects. In this paper, heterogeneous integration (HI) in CPO is discussed. Multi-physics packaging is exemplified with two cases. Challenges in HI technologies are reviewed and corresponding mitigation methods are provided, including (1) thermal crosstalk within the electrical domain and between the electrical and the optical interaction, (2) SIPI of wide-and-slow and narrow-and-fast channel links, and (3) pros and cons of interposer material. Integrated photonics part is introduced and is composed of (1) light sources, (2) optical coupling strategies, (3) fiber attach schemes with advanced packaging, and (4) integrated optical technologies, e.g. novel microlens, optical TSV, 3D waveguide, and optical 3DIC. This article aims to identify the key HI challenges in CPO and points out the potential solutions for future CPO system advancement.

sources.title: 2.5D co-packaged optical I/O chipsets on a SiON/Si interposer for 4 $\times$ 100G optical interconnection
sources.abstract: Optical I/O technologies have emerged as a potential industrial solution for high-performance data interconnection in AI/ML computing acceleration. While optical I/Os are deployed at the edge of computational chips by co-packaged optics (CPO), flexible and high-performance integration architectures need to be explored to address system-level challenges. In this work, we present and experimentally demonstrate a SiON/Si-based optical interposer that integrates high-bandwidth and energy-efficient optical I/O chipsets. High-performance photonic and electronic components are co-packaged on the interposer, leading to low-loss, signal-integrity-friendly, and thermally efficient characteristics. The optical interposer incorporates low-loss SiON photonic circuits to realize scalable waveguide routing and wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) with polarization-insensitive operation and high fabrication tolerance, while supporting flip-chip integration with InP-based active devices, including electro-absorption modulated lasers (EMLs) and photodetectors (PDs). Based on this architecture, a 400-Gb/s single-fiber optical transceiver is implemented and experimentally evaluated. Clear eye diagrams and high receiver sensitivity demonstrate reliable high-speed data transmission, which offers scalable, high-bandwidth optical I/Os in future high-performance computational clusters.

sources.title: 3D Optoelectronics and Co-Packaged Optics: Innovations, Challenges, and Future Trends
sources.venue: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
sources.abstract: Co-packaged optics (CPO) and three-dimensional (3D) optoelectronics represent a new frontier in high-speed data communication, targeting the rising demands for bandwidth, energy efficiency, and low latency in data centers, artificial intelligence (AI), and high-performance computing (HPC). This review examines the progression from pluggable optics to integrated photonic solutions, highlighting breakthroughs in silicon photonics, heterogeneous integration, and advanced packaging methods such as 2.5D interposers, Embedded Multi-die Inter- connect Bridge (EMIB), and 3D stacking. These innovations promise significant reductions in power consumption and notable gains in bandwidth density, yet thermal management, manufacturing yields, and alignment precision remain key challenges. Applications span hyperscale data centers, quantum networks, automotive lidar, and aerospace communications, illustrating the wide-reaching impact of these emerging technologies. The paper concludes by emphasizing future research directions and collaborative efforts needed to address remaining barriers and fully harness the transformative potential of integrated photonic- electronic systems.

sources.title: Ultrafast laser processing of glass waveguide substrates for multi-fiber connectivity in co-packaged optics
sources.abstract: High bandwidth demanding applications such as high-performance computing and hyperscale datacenters are drivers for co-packaged optics, which aims to bring optical signals as close as possible to the electrical computing chips by integrating the electro-optic transceivers and ASICs on the same package substrate. These next-generation switches require advanced fiber-to-chip connectivity and novel packaging concepts to enable sufficient power and cost savings. As such, low-loss, high bandwidth, and high fiber-counts are required at the photonic chip interface. In this work, these challenges are addressed by enabling the multi-fiber push-on (MPO) interface at the edge of integrated glass waveguide substrates and thus leverages the existing fiber connector eco-system. An ultrafast laser process is used to singulate glass wafers into individual photonic chips leaving optical-quality end-facets with <1 μm flatness over the 6.5 mm wide connector region thereby directly enabling low-loss fiber-to-chip edge-coupling. To overcome the high-costs and complex photonic packaging associated with active alignment of the fiber connectors to the glass waveguide interfaces, ultrafast laser-ablated features are accurately positioned on the glass substrate to enable self-alignment of the MPO connector guide-pins resulting in a passive alignment approach. Subsequent mating and de-mating of the MPO connector to the glass waveguide interface yields on average a 0.19 dB increase in the coupling loss compared to using active alignment.

sources.title: Thermomechanical and Compression Analyses for Large-Scale Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) Assembly
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Components Packaging and Manufacturing Technology
sources.abstract: With the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and other high-performance computing, the data transmission bandwidth in data centers has increased to 51.2 Tbps and will double every two years. The traditional pluggable optical modules have difficulty in satisfying the requirements. Co-packaged optics (CPO) integrates ASICs and optical engines (OEs) on the same substrate, providing a low energy loss and high throughput solution. However, the CPO structure is complicated and the package size is large. Therefore, the assembly-induced mechanical stresses and warpage of CPO are serious issues. In this article, assembly feasibility based on a$200\times 200$mm2 51.2-Tbps CPO was analyzed by a cross-scale simulation methodology with multiple mechanical stresses. First, the ASIC structure optimization of the CPO was carried out, and the CPO substrate was determined. Then, based on the above-optimized structure, the thermal reflow simulations of ASIC and mechanical compression simulations of OEs were conducted by the birth and death element method. The results showed that the stiffener ring in the ASIC package was optimized to be 3 mm in height and 15 mm in width. The 5-mm PCB was determined for the CPO substrate. The CPO substrate warpage under the socket after the thermal reflow was less than 0.05 mm and the maximum equivalent stresses of the ball grid array (BGA) in the whole assembly process were less than the yield strength of the SAC305 by submodel structure analysis. The socket terminal forces after mechanical compression were greater than 0.1 N. The analyzed results meet the process targets during the assembly of the CPO.

sources.title: Heterogeneous Integration Technology Drives the Evolution of Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), data centers, and high-performance computing (HPC) has increased the demand for large bandwidth, high energy efficiency, and high-density optical interconnects. Co-packaged optics (CPO) technology offers a promising solution by integrating photonic integrated circuits (PICs) directly within or close to electronic integrated circuit (EIC) packages. This paper explores the evolution of CPO performance from various perspectives, including fan-out wafer level packaging (FOWLP), through-silicon via (TSV)-based packaging, through-glass via (TGV)-based packaging, femtosecond laser direct writing waveguides, ion-exchange glass waveguides, and optical coupling. Micro ring resonators (MRRs) are a high-density integration solution due to their compact size, excellent energy efficiency, and compatibility with CMOS processes. However, traditional thermal tuning methods face limitations such as high static power consumption and severe thermal crosstalk. To address these issues, non-volatile neuromorphic photonics has made breakthroughs using phase-change materials (PCMs). By combining the integrated storage and computing capabilities of photonic memory with the efficient optoelectronic interconnects of CPO, this deep integration is expected to work synergistically to overcome material, integration, and architectural challenges, driving the development of a new generation of computing hardware with high energy efficiency, low latency, and large bandwidth.

sources.title: Machine-learning-driven optimization of vertical fiber-to-chip coupling system for co-packaged optics and in-package optical I/O applications
sources.abstract: Efficient light coupling in photonic integrated circuits (PICs) is vital for co-packaged optics (CPO) and in-package optical I/O (OIO). Grating couplers in PICs offer a viable solution for vertical coupling to a fiber attachment above the chip but are sensitive to fabrication and alignment variations. Using micro-optics, like collimating micro-lenses, can mitigate these issues but adds system complexity. Designing such systems necessitates simulating light propagation across different scales, from the sub-wavelength feature size of the grating coupler to the millimeter scale of the micro-optics and fiber attachment above. We propose an automated optimization workflow driven by state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms that combines optical simulation techniques suitable for these scales. This workflow also includes robustness analysis to capture variations from fiber assembly, fabrication, and material errors, providing insights into key variations affecting yield in the manufacture process.

sources.title: Integrated Assembly Process For Pluggable Fiber Connector For Co-Packaged Optics
sources.venue: IEEE Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)
sources.abstract: Detachable optical connectors for I/O chiplets have emerged as a de-facto requirement to address key challenges in co-packaged photonics manufacturing yield and field serviceability. They decouple optical interconnect assembly yield from the final package, enabling full functional testing of "known-good" dies (KGDs) and eliminating the yield loss risks associated with last step permanent fiber attachment.The core of Photonic Fabric (PF) chiplet is a Si-photonics interface. To enable good thermal stability at that interface, PF uses Germanium-Silicon (GeSi) Electro-Absorption Modulators (EAMs). Optical path is provided through a lens optical block that is attached topside of the photonics integrated circuit (PIC) before the overmold process, using index-matching adhesive. The mold grind process exposes the lens block and the top die(s) for the subsequent fiber attach unit (FAU) receptacle attach.The assembly process and material selection must hence ensure: 1) optical adhesives with low optical loss; 2) submicron alignment and strict control of bonding line thickness keep-out zones, even with high aspect ratio optical blocks associated with high fiber channel counts; 3) compatibility with reflow and reliability requirements.In this paper, we present material selection, tolerance analyses, and assembly processes for PF chiplet with detachable optical connector, along with preliminary optical and reliability characterizations.

sources.title: A Smart, Sensor-Augmented Probe Card for Wafer-Level Photonic Testing of Co-Packaged Optics Devices
sources.abstract: The transition from electrical to optical interconnects, enabled by the adoption of co-packaged optics (CPO) in advanced processors, is accelerating the scale-up to high volumes and redefining wafer-level test requirements. As optical interfaces migrate closer to the compute die, an increasing share of functional characterization must occur at the probe, where stringent sub-micron alignment, the mechanical stability necessary to preserve optical coupling against dynamic disturbances, and opto-electrical co-validation introduce new technical challenges. Ensuring repeatable and precise fiber-array-unit (FAU) engagement at the wafer level is therefore essential to enable scalable manufacturing of photonic-enabled processors. This paper introduces the EclipsePhotonic probe card, which embeds the Eclipse Dynamic piezoelectric positioning mechanism into a standard vertical-needle probe head as a route toward six-degree-of-freedom FAU manipulation with nanometric positioning accuracy. This architecture is designed to support repeatable coupling to on-wafer photonic structures without requiring specialized probe-head designs, thereby reducing integration complexity and addressing alignment-related yield risks. The platform is also intended to support multi-site electrical and optical probing, providing a path toward parallel test execution once the corresponding layout, optical-routing, and validation constraints are satisfied. A core innovation of the platform is its embedded sensor network, which integrates low- and higher-frequency displacement sensors, relative displacement sensors, and temperature sensors around a microcontroller-based supervisor. The vibration sensor fulfills a dual operational role: it detects environmental and test-cell disturbances that may have influenced optical coupling, providing essential context for binning decisions or targeted retest, and it contributes to probe card lifecycle monitoring by ensuring that the mechanical signature of the probe card remains within a validated operational “swim lane” throughout its service life. Recently published characterization of the underlying Eclipse Dynamic alignment engine shows that, in the production-optimized high-speed regime with effective hysteresis compensation, the Fixed Gradient routine provides the best normalized trade-off among the evaluated routines, with a normalized alignment cost of 1.44 a.u., 95.8% convergence reliability, and 99.4% of the global maximum optical coupling. These values should be interpreted as inherited algorithmic benchmarking results rather than as absolute wall-clock performance of the fully integrated sensor-augmented platform.

sources.title: Integration Methods for Co-Packaged Optics using Sin-to-Polymer Waveguide Coupling
sources.venue: OptoElectronics and Communications Conference and International Conference on Photonics in Switching and Computing (OECC/PSC)
sources.abstract: We present broadband silicon-nitride to polymer waveguide adiabatic coupling interfaces with sub-1 dB loss around 1310 nm, validated using two integration methods: lithography and flip-chip bonding, achieving sub-2dB chip-to-chip and chip-to-fiber coupling loss. Keywords: Photonic integrated circuits, Photonics-Electronics integration, Packaging technology of photonic devices and circuits, Tapered and grating waveguides for optical coupling, Si photonic and heterogeneous platform, On-board optics and co-packaged optics for high-capacity interconnects

sources.title: Design of Silicon Photonics Metasurface Enabling Optical Interfacing for Co-Packaged Optics
sources.abstract: The exponential growth of AI-driven data traffic necessitates the evolution of Data Center Networks toward high bandwidths and sub-microsecond latency. While co-packaged optics (CPO) offer a pathway to reduced energy consumption and increased capacity, they introduce significant challenges in optical chip coupling and packaging complexity. This study explores monolithically integrated metasurfaces as an alternative for optical interfaces, potentially reducing the need for bulky external microlens arrays or extremely precise mechanical alignment. We design an amorphous silicon (a-Si) metasurface on a Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) platform operating at 1310 nm. By spatially mapping nanopillar radii to satisfy a spherical phase profile, we achieved near-vertical beam emission with an emission angle of 0.88° focused at a focal length of 98.99 μm. Broadband characterization across a 20 nm band confirms stable focusing and a confined spot size with moderate roll-off toward the band edges. The sensitivity of the emission profile of the device to fabrication imperfections in pillar radius, height, and sidewall taper is quantified. The coupling to a polymer-based optical redistribution layer (ORDL) is also studied, and the corresponding modal analysis demonstrates a maximum coupling efficiency of 68.2% into an SU-8 polymer waveguide. Tolerance analysis results reveal deterioration of 0.9 dB and 0.4 dB for ±0.6 μm horizontal and ±1.5 μm vertical misalignment respectively, making the interface compatible with relaxed alignment assembly assumptions, although experimental packaging validation remains required. The methodology is further validated at 1550 nm, demonstrating its applicability across telecom bands. These results suggest that integrated metasurfaces may simplify the packaging stack and enhance density for next-generation CPO links by providing precise, on-chip wavefront manipulation.

findings.claim: A 2025 review lists thermal management, manufacturing yield and alignment precision as unresolved key challenges for CPO and 3D optoelectronics, even as it describes the power and bandwidth-density gains as promised.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single review abstract. It names the challenges but gives no quantified yield or thermal limits. The gains are described as 'promise', not as demonstrated at production scale.
findings.supporting_excerpt: thermal management, manufacturing yields, and alignment precision remain key challenges

findings.claim: Large-format CPO packages carry mechanical risk. A 200x200 mm, 51.2 Tbps CPO assembly is described as having serious assembly-induced stress and warpage problems. The mitigation shown (stiffener ring, 5 mm PCB substrate) rests on cross-scale simulation, not on measured hardware in the abstract.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The risk is stated in the abstract, but the abstract is truncated. The mitigation evidence is simulation only, and the paper has only 3 citations. Whether the simulated warpage (<0.05 mm) holds in volume manufacturing is a gap, not a demonstrated failure.
findings.supporting_excerpt: the assembly-induced mechanical stresses and warpage of CPO are serious issues

findings.claim: Permanent fiber attachment is a yield and serviceability risk. A 2026 ECTC paper calls detachable optical connectors a de-facto requirement, because last-step permanent fiber attachment can destroy the yield of an otherwise good package. The same paper offers only preliminary optical and reliability characterization of its connector approach.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single conference abstract from one chiplet design (Photonic Fabric). It is not independently confirmed, and its connector solution adds new tolerance demands: submicron alignment, bonding-line control, and reflow compatibility. Field replaceability of a connector on a shared package is not shown to be solved.
findings.supporting_excerpt: eliminating the yield loss risks associated with last step permanent fiber attachment

findings.claim: Optical coupling and alignment remain fragile, and no approach looks settled. Grating couplers are sensitive to fabrication and alignment variation. Micro-optics fix that but add system complexity. Metasurface couplers are only at design and simulation stage, with a maximum modelled coupling efficiency of 68.2% and sensitivity to pillar-radius, height and sidewall error.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Three independent abstracts describe alignment or fabrication sensitivity as the problem, and each proposes a different fix: ML-optimised micro-optics, a metasurface, and a piezo-positioned probe card. The metasurface paper is a design study with no fabricated device. The probe-card paper describes a platform 'designed to' and 'intended to' deliver capabilities, and the ML paper is a workflow proposal. The cited papers have 0-1 citations each. This is a judgement about how mature the solutions are, not a measured failure.

findings.claim: Reported low-loss coupling demonstrations are laboratory results, and the abstracts show a loss budget that accumulates. Sub-2 dB chip-to-chip and chip-to-fiber loss is achieved with polymer waveguides. MPO mate/demate adds about 0.19 dB on average. None of the abstracts report production yield statistics, long-term reliability or cost.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstracts give per-interface losses measured on small samples. Loss across a full link with many interfaces, and its variation across a wafer or lot, is not reported. The glass-substrate abstract is truncated. Absence of yield and cost data is a gap in the evidence, not proof of failure.

findings.claim: Micro-ring resonators, a high-density modulator option for CPO, face drawbacks in conventional thermal tuning: high static power and severe thermal crosstalk. The proposed remedy, phase-change-material neuromorphic photonics, is described only as 'expected' to help.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is one review abstract. The PCM remedy is prospective and unquantified, and tying it to CPO is speculative. The tuning power penalty works against CPO's energy-efficiency case.
findings.supporting_excerpt: traditional thermal tuning methods face limitations such as high static power consumption and severe thermal crosstalk

findings.claim: The CPO integration landscape is fragmented, with VCSEL versus silicon photonics, 2D/2.5D/3D packaging, FOWLP, TSV and TGV paths, and different coupling schemes all competing. This raises the risk of ecosystem and standards fragmentation and of design lock-in for any single process or supplier.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The reviews catalogue many parallel approaches and list standardization as an open area. They do not rank the approaches or analyse supplier concentration. Convergence timing is not shown in the abstracts, so the fragmentation risk is inferred, not measured.

findings.claim: New wafer-level test requirements add manufacturing cost and complexity. Optical interfaces near the compute die force functional characterisation into the probe step, which needs sub-micron fiber-array alignment and mechanical stability. A proposed piezo-positioned probe card is presented as a path, with parallel testing contingent on constraints still to be met.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: One 2026 article and one conference paper, both with 0 citations. The probe-card abstract is truncated and gives no throughput or repeatability data. Test cost and throughput impact are not quantified, which is a gap.

hype_flags: 'Disruptive' and 'transformative potential' framing in reviews: the abstracts give no head-to-head, quantified comparison against improving pluggable optics.
The claim that pluggable optics growth is 'unsustainable' rests on a traffic-growth argument in one review, with no cost, power or reliability benchmarks in the abstract.
'Significant reductions in power consumption' (3D/CPO review): stated as a promise, not quantified in the abstract.
Synergy between PCM neuromorphic photonics and CPO is speculative, with no integrated demonstration.
Wide application lists (quantum networks, automotive lidar, aerospace) dilute focus and are not supported by evidence on CPO cost or maturity.
Low-loss coupling headlines (about 1 dB, sub-2 dB) come from lab demonstrations without yield or reliability data.
'Widely regarded as promising' is an appeal to consensus, not evidence.

finding.claim: S2 and S12 are labelled verified_fact, but they restate the stance of a single, non-peer-reviewed arXiv position paper. The paper itself says it is arguing a thesis and offers a prediction about what will be 'decisive'. Neither is an empirical result. S12 in particular is a forecast about adoption and should not be carried as a verified fact.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the source is an argument. The abstract reports no data, and only the abstract was available. Both findings rest on this one preprint, so they should be downgraded to ai_interpretation or forecast and corroborated by independent work.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Here, we argue that co-packaged optics should not be viewed as a component-level optimization, but as an architectural commitment that reshapes the boundaries between photonics, electronics, and system design.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S1 and S10 present CPO's bandwidth-density, energy-efficiency and size/weight/power benefits as verified facts. The cited review abstracts report no quantified, measured comparison against pluggable optics. A 2025 review in the evidence set says the gains are only 'promised' and lists thermal management, yield and alignment as unresolved. Cost and deployed-system evidence are also absent. The benefits are claimed or expected, not demonstrated at system level in these sources.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: src_8bc0d86153 says CPO is 'widely regarded as a promising solution', which describes consensus rather than measurement. src_e674fc828f asserts 'distinct benefits' with no numbers in the abstract. The benefit claims should be labelled as claimed or expected and paired with the open challenges.
finding.supporting_excerpt: These innovations promise significant reductions in power consumption and notable gains in bandwidth density, yet thermal management, manufacturing yields, and alignment precision remain key challenges.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 says 'multiple independent abstracts' converge on packaging as the limiting factor. The sources are not independent. The two glass-substrate papers appear to be the same platform (same title stem, same waveguide and cavity concept). The two SiN-to-polymer papers (src_8e7b74bf2d and the OECC abstract src_8372b0a8d6) look closely related, and the reviews overlap in scope. The claim that the device is not the limiting factor is also not tested in these abstracts. At least one source in the evidence set names device-level limits, such as microring thermal tuning with high static power and severe thermal crosstalk. The retrieved set is also heavily weighted toward packaging, which biases the convergence.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Apparent agreement may come from repeated work by the same groups and from search selection, not independent confirmation. Device-level issues such as microring thermal behaviour remain a limiting factor alongside packaging. The conclusion 'rather than the photonic device itself' goes beyond what the abstracts compare.
finding.supporting_excerpt: However, traditional thermal tuning methods face limitations such as high static power consumption and severe thermal crosstalk.

finding.claim: S4 and S5 report best-case laboratory coupling losses ('minimum loss', 'near 1 dB') as if they described the technology. The same glass-platform abstract also reports an average connector loss of 0.83 dB, which S4 omits, so the end-to-end budget is larger than the headline figure. The abstracts give no yield statistics, repeatability data or long-term reliability data. S5 rests on an arXiv preprint and a short conference abstract, and its text calls for 'high-yield' interfacing as a requirement rather than a demonstrated result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Minimum-loss figures are the best of a set of trials. Further loss is added by the connector (0.83 dB here) and by MPO mate/demate, which src_02eb990d2e reports adds about 0.19 dB on average. Without yield or reliability data, 'experimentally validated' should not be read as manufacturing-ready.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Average connector loss of 0.83 dB was demonstrated with physical contact between fibers and IOX glass waveguides.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 is labelled verified_fact, but its 400 Gb/s and 9.65 dBm figures come entirely from simulation and link-level BER modelling, not from measured hardware. Reaching 400 Gb/s at 9.65 dBm is a modelled projection that depends on foundry process models and on a thermal-stability assessment that is also simulated. It is an arXiv preprint with no fabrication result.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: S6 does use the word 'simulated', but the verified_fact label and the specific numbers invite over-reading. The result is a design-stage projection. Microring modulators are also sensitive to thermal drift, which a simulation can under-represent.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We simulate and evaluate the performance of our proposed MRM-based coherent CPO (C2PO) transmitters using a foundry-provided commercial silicon photonics process
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 gives a 400-Gb/s single-fiber transceiver on a SiON/Si interposer as supporting evidence, but the abstract's 'reliable' and 'thermally efficient' wording rests only on eye diagrams and receiver sensitivity. No energy-per-bit, thermal, reliability or scaling data are reported. It is a 4x100G laboratory demonstration from an arXiv preprint, and it is not evidence of switch-scale CPO.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Eye diagrams and sensitivity show signal quality at one operating point. They do not show reliability, power efficiency or scalability, which the abstract claims in qualitative terms. The finding should carry a caveat that it is an unreviewed, single-demonstration result.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Clear eye diagrams and high receiver sensitivity demonstrate reliable high-speed data transmission, which offers scalable, high-bandwidth optical I/Os in future high-performance computational clusters.

limitations: Analysis rests on 12 titles and abstracts only (abstract_only); several abstracts are truncated, so key results and caveats may be missing.
The corpus is mostly reviews and component-level packaging or coupling papers. It has almost no system-level data on power, cost, field reliability, laser reliability or deployed products.
No papers were retrieved on competing alternatives (e.g., linear-drive pluggable optics, near-package optics, improved copper), so displacement risk cannot be assessed.

Several items are simulation or design-only (thermomechanical analysis, metasurface, ML coupling workflow). Several are very recent with 0-1 citations and no independent replication. Their peer-review status is not shown in the metadata, and none are arXiv preprints.
Reviews summarise vendor work (Intel, Broadcom, IBM) without independent verification. Supplier concentration and supply-chain risk are not covered by the papers.
Limited search coverage means results may under-represent negative or failed deployments, since such results are rarely published.
Only titles and abstracts were available. Several abstracts are truncated, and none of the full papers was read, so details that qualify these results may be missing.
Several cited papers are arXiv preprints without peer review, and some have no citation counts. I could not assess their reproducibility.
I did not challenge S3, S8 or S9. They are described accurately in the abstracts, and any remaining weakness is minor or already covered by the risk findings.
The evidence set is small (21 papers) and weighted toward packaging, so I could not test claims about competing technologies such as linear pluggable optics, or about cost and deployment.

sources.title: STRUCTURES AND METHODS FOR INTEGRATED OPTICS MICROELECTROMECHANICAL SYSTEMS [US20260339027A1]
sources.organization: MENARD FRANCOIS, BRIERE JONATHAN, BERARD MARTIN
sources.abstract: [0000]    Silicon Photonics is a candidate technology for adding integrated optics functionality, either passive or active optical waveguides) to integrated circuits by leveraging the economies of scale of the CMOS microelectronics industry and using materials for the waveguide core such as silicon nitride (Si<X>N<Y>) and silicon oxynitride (SiO<X>N<1-X>) for example. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) provide for movable platforms relative to the substrate allowing additional functionality to be added to a silicon circuit but also Silicon Photonics. Accordingly, by combining “fixed” waveguides formed upon a substrate with “movable” waveguides formed upon one or more movable or extendible platforms the inventors have established a series of Integrated Optics MEMS (IO-MEMS) elements based on Silicon Photonics. Such IO-MEMS include optical switches, optical attenuators, optical gates, optical switch matrices, configurable wavelength division multiplexer/demultiplexer devices, phase shifters, phase modulators and amplitude modulators exploiting suspended platforms and beams.

sources.title: OPTICAL INTERCONNECT MONITORING AND FAULT DETECTION IN DISTRIBUTED COMPUTING COMPONENTS [US20260322683A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A system for monitoring optical computing components is disclosed. The system may include processors and non-transitory computer-readable media comprising instructions. The system may receive optical measurements from optical interconnects internal to a distributed computing system, where the optical interconnects couple distributed computing components each having an associated optical communication device enabling optical communication at a package level. The system may receive performance metrics of the distributed computing components comprising workload activity, synchronization behavior, or thermal conditions. The system may input the optical measurements and performance metrics into an artificial intelligence model trained to predict potential faults. The system may determine a fault domain comprising a chiplet interface, an optical engine, a laser source, a coupler, or a reconfigurable optical path. The system may generate a message comprising a repair recommendation, an alert, or an automated corrective action based on the fault domain.

sources.title: CLOCK FORWARDING IN PACKAGED OPTICS LINKS [US20260312713A1]
sources.abstract: Conventional packaged optics systems recover clock from data signals using clock and data recovery circuitry, which introduces jitter. The recovered clock cannot perfectly track timing variations in the data signal because the recovery circuitry operates with finite bandwidth and response time. This timing misalignment reduces effective eye opening at the receiver and may require more powerful forward error correction schemes that consume additional power and introduce latency. The present disclosure addresses this problem by transmitting the clock on a dedicated wavelength channel through the same optical fiber as the data channels. Because the clock signal traverses the same optical medium and experiences similar propagation characteristics, the forwarded clock tracks jitter present in the data channels. This reduces effective jitter at the sampling instant and may eliminate gearbox circuitry otherwise required for rate conversion. These techniques may be applied to packaged optics architectures, including co-packaged optics and near-packaged optics configurations.

sources.title: Assay for Rapid Detection of Antibiotic Resistant Organisms [US20260308658A1]
sources.abstract: In a method for detecting a carbapenemase-producing organism (CPO), a bacterial sample is lysed and the lysate is incubated with a carbapenem. The carbapenem is then transferred a solution including bacterial growth medium, an indicator bacterial strain that is susceptible to the carbapenem, a protease, and a cell viability indicator that can be metabolized by the indicator bacterial strain. After an incubation period, a change in the cell viability indicator confirms that the bacterial sample comprises a CPO, and no change in the cell viability indicator confirms that the bacterial sample does not include a CPO. A kit for an assay for detecting a CPO includes a lysis solution, a carbapenem, a bacterial growth medium, an indicator bacterial strain that is susceptible to the carbapenem, a protease, and a cell viability indicator that is metabolizable by the indicator bacterial strain.

sources.title: Optoelectronic Devices Including Selectable Anode and Cathode Regions Able to Drive Coupled PMOS or NMOS Transistors in a Complementary Push-Pull Configuration [US20260301659A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Optoelectronic devices having simultaneously and independently addressable anode and cathode regions. They support a push-pull complementary transistor driving configuration that employs at least one PMOS transistor coupled to the p-type anode region and at least one NMOS transistor coupled to the n-type cathode region to drive each optoelectronic element in a complementary push-pull mode. Independent addressability of the cathode and anode is enabled by an electrically inactive p-type isolation region, which forms a depletion region with the n-type cathode to electrically isolate individual elements. The push-pull configuration provides enhanced switching speed, reduced static power dissipation, wider dynamic range, improved noise rejection, and greater design flexibility. The PMOS and NMOS transistors may be fabricated on a standard CMOS backplane wafer bonded to the optoelectronic element array, fully leveraging standard CMOS foundry capabilities for high-resolution micro-LED displays, detector arrays, data center optical interconnects, co-packaged optics, and optical transceiver arrays.

sources.title: Optical Switch with Fast Switching and Fast Transceiver Acquisition [US20260292375A1]
sources.abstract: This disclosure presents systems and methods for an optical circuit switch (OCS), optical burst switch (OBS), and hybrid OBS (HOBS) featuring microsecond-range reconfiguration times—critical for modern AI/ML workloads demanding both low latency and high bandwidth. By combining fast switching elements (e.g., silicon photonics) with burst-mode transceivers that reduce acquisition from seconds to microseconds, the proposed architectures enable efficient data center interconnects. The design coordinates switch reconfiguration and transceiver lock-in through in-band or out-of-band control, minimizing overhead to under ten percent of each burst's duration. Additional optimizations—such as buffering packet headers, using a second wavelength for control signals, and employing partial DSP training—further boost performance while reducing power consumption. These fast optical switches support both short, frequent bursts (scale-up) and large, stable flows (scale-out), delivering high-throughput, low-latency connections suitable for AI/ML clusters, HPC environments, and other dynamic data center applications.

draft.summary: Research and patent activity on co-packaged optics (CPO) is rising fast: papers went from 84 to 150 between 2024 and 2025, and 2026 is up about 90% year to date. Patent publications are also rising (finding P1-P3). Company filings from Coherent, Lumentum, ASE, Ciena, AMD, Veeco and FormFactor show an ecosystem forming around AI datacenter interconnects (M1-M8). However, the science evidence is mostly laboratory demonstrations, simulations and reviews (S4, S5, S6, S7). Risk challenges note that system-level benefits versus pluggable optics, cost, yield and reliability are not demonstrated in the retrieved sources (C2, C4, R1, R5). The main uncertainty is whether packaging, thermal, alignment and serviceability problems can be solved at volume and cost. Research activity is not commercial success, and the filings do not isolate CPO-specific revenue.
draft.plain_summary: Co-packaged optics puts the light-based data connections right next to the computer chip, so AI datacenters can move data faster using less power. Research, patents and company activity are all growing quickly, but most proof so far comes from lab tests and company statements rather than large-scale use. The thing most likely to slow it down is the difficulty of building and testing these tightly packed parts reliably and cheaply.

missing_data: All agents ran, but the evidence has gaps: no measured system-level comparison of CPO versus pluggable optics (energy per bit, latency, cost).
No production yield, long-term reliability or cost data for any CPO packaging approach.
No named customers, order volumes, deployment counts or CPO-specific revenue in company filings.
No evidence on the status of standards or multi-vendor interoperability beyond a single position paper.
Competitive position and market share data are absent.
Company-level evidence for Marvell, Celestica and Broadcom comes only from social-media posts; the Lumentum acquisition report is unverified.

limitations: Science evidence is mostly abstracts, preprints and reviews; several 'verified' findings were challenged as simulation-based, single-source or best-case (C1-C6).
Retrieved papers appear weighted toward packaging, which may bias the apparent convergence on packaging as the bottleneck (C3).
Paper and patent counts measure activity, not commercial success; recent patent counts are undercounted due to publication delay.
Market findings from filing excerpts show company statements, not adoption; headline and social-media findings are unverified claims.
Price and timing metrics are risk context only, not entry-point or return signals.
